content: Imagine you are sitting in a moving train. You look out the window and see trees rushing backwards. But when you look at the passenger sitting next to you, they don't seem to be moving at all. How can you be moving and not moving at the exact same time?
Why do we say the trees are moving backwards? Are they really moving, or are you? If you were standing on the platform, what would the trees look like?

content.title: Frame of Reference
content.description: Visualizing motion from different observers' perspectives.

content: Motion is a change in position of an object over time. But here is the secret: motion is always relative! It depends on who is looking (the observer) and from where they are looking (the reference point).

question: A person is standing on a railway platform and watches a train speed by. To the person on the platform, the passengers inside the train are:

content: Think about the Earth. Is it moving right now? Yes, it's spinning and orbiting the sun. So, are you moving right now while sitting and reading this? Try explaining this to a friend using the idea of a 'reference point'.
Understanding motion is the first step to understanding everything in the universe, from how cars drive on roads to how planets orbit the sun. Later, we will connect this to force and gravity!

title: Mastery Challenge: The Moving Car
description: Next time you are in a car, pick an object outside and describe its motion relative to you, and then relative to the road. Notice the difference!

content: Always define your reference point before trying to describe motion. Without a reference point, motion has no meaning!
Thinking that an object can only be either moving or at rest. Remember, an object can be at rest relative to one thing (like your seat) and in motion relative to another (like the ground outside).
